title: Zacchaeus up a tree (Luke 19:1–10)
hook: a short, hated tax collector climbs a sycamore; Jesus invites himself for dinner

segments.voice: Yesterday, transfiguration: a face like the sun, and Peter wanting to build tents. Your line was you can't stay on the mountain. Who did you carry the light to? Now the road runs south, through Jericho. Day fifty-nine.

Remember being the short kid at a parade, or at the back of a concert, bouncing on your toes and seeing nothing but shoulders? This is Jericho, an old city on the road up to Jerusalem. Jesus is passing through, and the streets are packed. One man wants very badly to see him. His name is Zacchaeus. Luke says he's the chief among the publicans, the tax collectors, and he's rich. Before this story ends, the whole crowd will call him a sinner. Nobody's going to make room for him. And he's short. So a grown, wealthy, powerful, unpopular man runs ahead and does something undignified. Today, sycamore.
screen: `BOUNCING ON YOUR TOES.` → `A CROWD IN JERICHO.` → `A SHORT, RICH, HATED MAN.`

segments.voice: Luke says he "climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way." A sycamore fig, a wide, low tree with branches easy to climb, not the American sycamore. There he is, a rich official, sitting in a tree like a boy. And Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and says his name: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Luke doesn't say how he knows the name. And he doesn't wait for an invitation. He invites himself to dinner. Zacchaeus scrambles down and welcomes him joyfully. But the crowd grumbles, all of them, Luke says: "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." And then, before anyone asks him to, Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. The law of Moses asked a thief to pay back four sheep for one stolen sheep. Zacchaeus holds himself to the thief's standard, on his own. Notice the order. Jesus didn't say, change first, then I'll come. He called him by name, came to his house, and the change came after, freely. Then Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and gives a line some readers take as a summary of Luke's whole Gospel: "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." And a small irony some readers hear in his name, which they link to a Hebrew word for pure. The whole town called him a sinner. Jesus called him by his name.
screen: `UP A SYCAMORE FIG.` · `ZACCHAEUS, MAKE HASTE, AND COME DOWN.` · `THE CROWD GRUMBLES.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · then, large: `TO SEEK AND TO SAVE THAT WHICH WAS LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one thing you got wrong with someone. Not the worst thing you ever did. Something you could actually fix. Money you owe. A promise you broke. Credit you took that wasn't yours. A harsh word you never took back. Picture the person. Now picture what making it right would look like. Maybe a message, a payment, an apology, a phone call. Don't beat yourself up. Zacchaeus didn't. He just stood up and said what he'd do. If you pray, you can ask for the courage. The bell holds the time.
Sycamore. A wide, low fig tree with branches easy to climb, the one a rich, short, unpopular tax collector climbed just to see Jesus pass by.
Your line: he knows your name. Today, make one thing right that you got wrong. Start small, but start. Day fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Zacchaeus at the dedication of a church building, and it's a favorite in children's Sunday school, often with a song. Christians often point to it when speaking of restitution: making amends in practical ways.

fork.setup: you're Zacchaeus. Jesus has just come to your house, and the whole town is grumbling that he's eating with a sinner. what do you do?

fork.reveal: Zacchaeus stands and promises half to the poor and fourfold to anyone he's cheated. Jesus says: this day is salvation come to this house.

original.note: Greek form of a Hebrew name that some readers link to a word for pure: a small irony in a man everyone called a sinner.

trapdoor: what you thought: a children's story about a short man in a tree.
what it means: a hated man is called down by name and welcomed first, and he changes his life freely, after.
what a scholar hears: fourfold matches what the law of Moses asked of a sheep thief, so Zacchaeus holds himself to a thief's standard, and some readers hear the word pure in his name.

notes: Sycomore (KJV) = sycamore fig, Ficus sycomorus; confirm.
Fourfold restitution: Exodus 22:1 (four sheep for a sheep); confirm the link.
Name Zacchaeus from Hebrew Zakkai, 'pure, innocent'; confirm.

Luke 19:8 can be read in Greek as a present-tense habit ('I give') rather than a new promise; some scholars read Zacchaeus as defending his existing practice. The script follows the common reading of a new commitment.
Luke 19:1–10 is read at the dedication of a church in the Roman Rite; confirm.
